title: Barriers 2024 — Part A
source: WSU Y5 Barriers 2024 MCQ, student reconstruction; stems rewritten, tested point preserved

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy cannot weight-bear on his left leg. The limb is shortened and externally rotated. He is overweight and there is no clear history of trauma.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An overweight adolescent with a shortened, externally rotated leg and no trauma is SCFE. Because he cannot weight-bear this is an unstable slip: image with an AP pelvis and a cross-table (shoot-through) lateral — frog-leg positioning is avoided in unstable slips because the abduction and external rotation can complete the slip and cause avascular necrosis. Perthes is 4–8 years; transient synovitis is younger and post-viral.
questions.point: Limp with a shortened, externally rotated leg in an overweight 8–15-year-old is SCFE. If they cannot weight-bear the slip is unstable — use an AP pelvis and cross-table lateral, never a frog-leg lateral, which can complete the slip.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on metoprolol and dabigatran for AF is found collapsed. He hit his head in the garage a week ago and recovered quickly. BP 200/110, HR 50 irregular. He opens eyes and withdraws to pain, more weakly on the left than the right, with incomprehensible speech. The right pupil is dilated and poorly reactive and the eye is deviated down and out.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Elderly, anticoagulated, minor head injury a week ago, then delayed deterioration with a third-nerve palsy from uncal herniation — a subdural, now expanding. Extradural is acute, young, and follows a lucid interval of hours, not days.
questions.point: Delayed deterioration days after minor head injury in an anticoagulated elderly patient is a subdural haematoma; a blown pupil means uncal herniation and needs urgent neurosurgery.

questions.stem: A previously well 42-year-old woman with severe abdominal pain has a provisional diagnosis of acute cholecystitis and is awaiting surgical review.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate analgesia?
questions.explanation: Severe surgical pain gets titrated IV opioid — analgesia does not obscure the diagnosis or the signs. Codeine is unreliable (CYP2D6 variability). NSAIDs are genuinely effective in biliary pain and even reduce progression to cholecystitis, but are second-line here for severity and are limited by renal function, bleeding risk and age.
questions.point: Severe acute abdominal pain is treated with titrated IV morphine — analgesia does not mask surgical signs, and codeine is unreliable.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a non-healing wound on her thigh nine months after minor trauma. The site was burned in childhood, requiring hospitalisation but not grafting.
questions.lead: What is the most likely pathology?
questions.explanation: A Marjolin ulcer — SCC arising in an old burn scar or chronic wound. Biopsy any non-healing lesion in scar tissue.
questions.point: A non-healing ulcer in an old burn scar or chronic wound is a Marjolin ulcer — squamous cell carcinoma — until biopsied.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman noticed sudden left hearing loss and tinnitus on waking three days ago. No vertigo, pain or discharge. Otoscopy is normal. Weber lateralises to the right ear.
questions.lead: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Weber lateralises away from the affected ear in sensorineural loss (towards it in conductive). Sudden SNHL is an emergency — high-dose steroids within days.
questions.point: Weber lateralises to the good ear in sensorineural loss and to the bad ear in conductive loss; sudden SNHL needs urgent high-dose steroids.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has 6 months of worsening low back pain. ALP 700 (30–300), calcium 2.4 (2.15–2.5), phosphate 1.0 (0.8–1.45), PSA 2. Lumbar X-ray reports cortical thickening and sclerosis encasing the vertebral margins with vertical trabecular thickening.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Markedly raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphate and 'picture-frame' sclerotic vertebrae is Paget's. Myeloma is lytic, not sclerotic, and runs a normal ALP — that is the discriminator, not the calcium (raised in only about a quarter of myeloma at diagnosis). A PSA of 2 makes prostatic sclerotic metastases unlikely, though it does not formally exclude them.
questions.point: Very high ALP with normal calcium and phosphate plus sclerotic, thickened 'picture-frame' vertebrae = Paget disease; myeloma raises calcium with a normal ALP.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has weeks of loose stools three times daily with intermittent blood, preceded by months of constipation, reduced appetite and 5 kg weight loss. PR confirms blood.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Change in bowel habit + rectal bleeding + weight loss at 60 is colorectal cancer until colonoscopy says otherwise. Diverticular bleeding is painless and large-volume without weight loss.
questions.point: Altered bowel habit with rectal bleeding and weight loss over 50 is colorectal cancer until excluded by colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has a dull ache and a firm intratesticular mass, hypoechoic on ultrasound.
questions.lead: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
questions.explanation: Diagnosis and treatment are the same operation: inguinal orchidectomy. Any trans-scrotal approach risks seeding the inguinal lymphatics, which the testis does not otherwise drain to.
questions.point: A solid intratesticular mass is diagnosed by radical inguinal orchidectomy — never trans-scrotal biopsy, which seeds inguinal nodes outside the normal para-aortic drainage.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 60-year-old man with no family history asks about bowel cancer screening.
questions.lead: What is appropriate per Australian guidelines?
questions.explanation: Average risk: iFOBT every 2 years. Since July 2024 eligibility starts at 45, but 45–49-year-olds must request their first kit; automatic invitations run from 50 to 74. Colonoscopy is for a positive FOBT or elevated familial risk.
questions.point: Australian bowel screening: iFOBT 2-yearly, eligible from 45 (request-only at 45–49), automatically invited 50–74; colonoscopy only for a positive FOBT or increased familial risk.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has insidious jaundice and a vague epigastric mass. Bilirubin, ALP, GGT and ALT are all raised.
questions.lead: Which bilirubin fraction predominates?
questions.explanation: Cholestatic LFTs from a mass (pancreatic head) mean obstruction of conjugated bilirubin's outflow — dark urine, pale stools. Unconjugated excess is haemolysis or Gilbert's.
questions.point: Obstructive jaundice (raised ALP/GGT, mass, pale stools, dark urine) is conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; unconjugated excess means haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old primigravida has rupture of membranes at 32 weeks with no pain. Afebrile, HR 90, cephalic, clear fluid pooling on speculum. Transfer to a tertiary unit is arranged.
questions.lead: Which treatment is most appropriate while transfer occurs?
questions.explanation: PPROM before 34 weeks: erythromycin to prolong latency and reduce chorioamnionitis, plus corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity. Amoxicillin/co-amoxiclav is avoided (NEC risk).
questions.point: PPROM before 34 weeks: erythromycin plus antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone); avoid co-amoxiclav because of NEC risk.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old primigravida has just delivered vaginally after an uncomplicated pregnancy. No medications were given at delivery.
questions.lead: What should be administered now?
questions.explanation: Active management of the third stage — prophylactic oxytocin with delivery of the anterior shoulder or immediately after birth — reduces PPH. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and second-line.
questions.point: Active third-stage management: prophylactic oxytocin at or immediately after delivery reduces PPH; ergometrine is second-line and contraindicated in hypertension.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 12 weeks: blood group O negative, antibody screen negative, Hb 112 (120–150), MCV 82, rubella immune, other serology negative.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Rh-negative and non-sensitised: routine prophylactic anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks (Australia retains the two-dose 625 IU schedule), plus after any sensitising event and postnatally if the baby is RhD positive. The Hb of 112 with an MCV of 82 is not dismissible as haemodilution at 12 weeks — that is a second/third-trimester phenomenon — so ferritin should also be checked, but anti-D scheduling is the answer here.
questions.point: RhD-negative, antibody-negative women get anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks in Australia, plus after sensitising events. Haemodilution belongs to the second and third trimesters — a low-normal Hb with low MCV at 12 weeks warrants a ferritin.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old primigravida with pre-pregnancy BMI 36 has an OGTT at 26 weeks: 2-hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L (ADIPS 2025 threshold ≥9.0).
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Diabetes educator and dietitian review with home glucose monitoring
questions.explanation: GDM starts with lifestyle, education and self-monitoring; pharmacotherapy (insulin first-line in Australia, metformin acceptable) only if targets are not met within 1–2 weeks.
questions.point: Newly diagnosed GDM: dietitian/educator plus home glucose monitoring first; insulin (or metformin) only if targets are not met on lifestyle within 1–2 weeks.

questions.stem: A baby rolls in both directions but needs support to sit. He reaches out and transfers objects from one hand to the other with a palmar grasp but has no pincer grip. He babbles without words, holds his bottle when feeding, and shows no anxiety towards the examiner.
questions.lead: What is his developmental age?
questions.explanation: Rolling, palmar transfer, babble, no pincer, no stranger anxiety = 6 months. By 9 months: sits unsupported, pincer developing, stranger anxiety. By 12: single words, cruising.
questions.point: 6 months = rolls, transfers hand to hand, babbles, no pincer grip, no stranger anxiety; 9 months adds sitting unsupported, pincer grip and stranger anxiety.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with two days of coryza develops a harsh barking cough, worse at night, with loud inspiratory noise when distressed. Temperature 38°C, pink and alert.
questions.lead: What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Barking cough with stridor on distress in a well toddler is croup — parainfluenza. Hib epiglottitis is toxic, drooling and stridor at rest; RSV is bronchiolitis (wheeze).
questions.point: Barking cough with inspiratory stridor in a well toddler is viral croup (parainfluenza) — oral dexamethasone; epiglottitis (Hib) is toxic and drooling.

questions.stem: A thin 10-month-old is below the 5th centile for weight and height with head circumference on the 90th. He has a prominent forehead and broad wrists and ankles.
questions.lead: Which deficiency explains this?
questions.explanation: Frontal bossing, widened wrists and ankles (metaphyseal flaring), poor growth — rickets. Vitamin C is scurvy (bleeding gums, bruising); A is night blindness.
questions.point: Frontal bossing, widened wrists/ankles and poor growth in an infant = rickets (vitamin D deficiency); check 25-OH vitamin D, calcium, phosphate, ALP.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old is drowsy and febrile (39.7°C) with capillary refill 4 seconds and a purpuric rash on the limbs. Fontanelle is flat. IV access is in and a saline bolus is given.
questions.lead: What is the next step?
options: Blood cultures then wait for results
questions.explanation: Fever, purpura and shock is meningococcal sepsis: give IV ceftriaxone immediately, taking blood cultures at the same time only if they cause no delay. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated while the child is shocked or coagulopathic, and must never hold up antibiotics.
questions.point: Febrile child with purpura and shock = meningococcaemia — IV ceftriaxone immediately; lumbar puncture is contraindicated while shocked or coagulopathic.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old presents with pallor and lethargy during a URTI. His father had chronic anaemia and a childhood splenectomy. He is jaundiced with splenomegaly. Hb 59 (100–140), WCC and platelets normal, reticulocytes 12% (0.5–1.5%).
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Haemolysis (jaundice, high retics, splenomegaly) with an autosomal dominant family history and a splenectomised parent is spherocytosis. G6PD is X-linked and episodic with oxidants; thalassaemia major presents by 6–12 months with microcytosis and no retic surge.
questions.point: Haemolytic anaemia with splenomegaly and an autosomal dominant family history (parent with splenectomy) is hereditary spherocytosis; G6PD is X-linked and oxidant-triggered.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has four months of low mood, tearfulness, anergia, hypersomnia (10 hours a night) and 5 kg weight gain.
questions.lead: Which investigation should be performed before starting an antidepressant?
questions.explanation: Weight gain, hypersomnia and fatigue overlap with hypothyroidism — exclude it before labelling depression. TFTs are part of the standard first-presentation screen.
questions.point: New depression with weight gain, hypersomnia and fatigue: check TFTs (and FBC, B12/folate, glucose) before starting an antidepressant — hypothyroidism mimics it.
